client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. My team is already short-staffed, and then out of nowhere they assigned me this massive project with a deadline that feels almost impossible to meet. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because at the end of the day the workload is still going to be there when I leave this office.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds genuinely heavy, and I can hear in your voice a kind of quiet exhaustion — like you've been holding this weight for a while and aren't sure where to set it down. You're right that talking won't erase the deadline, but I'm curious about that thought that it "won't change anything" — because sometimes the way we're thinking about an overwhelming situation can make it feel even more impossible than it actually is. Would you be open to exploring what feels most unmanageable about this project, so we can start to break it into something a little less all-or-nothing?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess what feels most unmanageable is that I don't even know where to start — every time I try to think about the project, my mind just kind of freezes up and I end up doing nothing, which then makes me feel worse about myself. And honestly, part of me is skeptical that breaking it into smaller pieces is going to help, because even the smaller pieces feel overwhelming when I think about how little time I have. It's like no matter how I slice it, there's just too much.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of tension in your voice — tells me your mind might actually be racing even more than the words let on, even if it feels like freezing on the outside. That cycle you're describing, where the overwhelm leads to paralysis, which then leads to self-criticism, is really common and really exhausting — but it's also worth noticing that "I did nothing" is probably not the whole truth, because staying functional under this much pressure *is* something. I wonder if we could gently challenge that thought that "no matter how I slice it, there's too much" — is there any evidence of a time you've navigated something that felt impossible at first, even imperfectly?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, yeah, there was a time about two years ago when we were short-staffed and I had to cover for two people at once, and somehow I got through it. But that feels different to me, because back then I had a manager who actually checked in and helped me prioritize, and now I feel pretty much on my own with this. So I'm not sure that example really counts, because the conditions were just so different.
therapist: It's really interesting that you found that example almost immediately, and yet there's a part of you that's working hard to dismiss it — I notice even in how you're speaking there's a kind of tension, like you're reaching for hope but then pulling back from it. The support from your manager mattered, absolutely, but the one who actually did the work under enormous pressure was *you*, and that capability didn't disappear when he or she did. What would it look like to ask for even a small amount of that kind of prioritization support now — whether from a colleague, your current manager, or even just building it into our work together here?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Asking my current manager for help feels really uncomfortable, because honestly I don't think they even fully understand how much is on my plate right now, and I worry that bringing it up will make me look like I can't handle the workload. There's also this guilt I carry around, like I should just be able to figure it out on my own without needing to ask for support. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it's a really strong feeling.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, almost carefully, like you were bracing for judgment — actually tells me this belief runs really deep, and I want to gently name it: the idea that needing support means you're failing is a really common but really unfair standard that you likely wouldn't apply to a colleague in your exact situation. You even noticed yourself that it sounds irrational out loud, which is actually a really important moment of insight — that gap between what you *know* and what you *feel* is exactly where we can do some work. What do you think that belief that you "should figure it out alone" is protecting you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think it's protecting me from feeling like a burden, or from giving people a reason to see me as less capable than they think I am. There's this fear that if I show any cracks, people will start questioning whether I deserve to be in the role I'm in. It's exhausting to hold that up all the time, but letting it go feels scarier than just keeping it together on my own.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, almost quietly, like you were letting something fragile out into the open — matches exactly how heavy that burden sounds, and I want you to know that what you just described takes real courage to articulate. That fear of being seen as less capable has a name in CBT — it's often called impostor-related thinking, and it works by convincing us that our value is always one visible crack away from collapsing, which is an exhausting and ultimately unprovable standard to live by. I'm curious — if a colleague you respected came to you and admitted they were struggling under an impossible workload, would *you* see them as less capable, or would you see someone being honest and human?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: No, honestly, if a colleague came to me like that I'd probably respect them more for being upfront about it rather than letting things fall apart quietly. But I think the difference is that I can extend that kind of understanding to other people way more easily than I can to myself, and I don't really know why that is. It makes sense when you lay it out that way, but knowing it and actually feeling it are just really different things for me.
therapist: The way you said that — softly, quickly, like the words were coming from somewhere tender — tells me this landed somewhere real for you, even if it doesn't yet *feel* true in your body. That gap you named, between knowing something and feeling it, is actually one of the most honest and important things a person can recognize about themselves, and it's not a flaw — it just means this belief has been with you long enough that it's going to need more than one conversation to loosen. What do you think it would take, even in a small way, to start practicing the same compassion toward yourself that you so naturally offer to others?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think part of what it would take is just catching myself in those moments when I'm being really harsh toward myself and trying to pause, but honestly that feels easier said than done because those thoughts move so fast I barely notice them before they've already done their damage. I guess I could try to ask myself what I'd say to a colleague in my situation, but I worry I'll just dismiss it as a mental exercise that doesn't really touch the feeling underneath. It's like I can see the door but I'm not sure I actually know how to open it yet.
therapist: The way you're speaking — quickly, with a kind of high, tight energy in your voice, even as the words themselves feel uncertain and subdued — tells me there's more distress underneath this than you might even be fully aware of in this moment. That image you used, seeing the door but not knowing how to open it, is actually a really meaningful sign of progress, because not long ago in our conversation you weren't even sure the door existed. The "colleague question" isn't just a mental exercise — it's a practice, and like any practice it starts clumsy and slow before it becomes natural, so I'd gently push back on dismissing it before you've even tried it once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and I think you're right that I was dismissing it before even giving it a real chance, which is kind of a pattern for me actually. I guess I could try it this week when things get bad at work, just notice the harsh thought and ask myself what I'd tell a colleague, even if it feels hollow at first. I just worry that in the middle of a stressful moment at work, I won't have the mental space to even remember to do it.
therapist: The way you're speaking — soft but quick, like someone trying to hold something together carefully — tells me there's still a quiet worry underneath even this small step forward, and that's okay. You've just named something really significant though: that dismissing things before trying them is a *pattern*, which means you're not just solving a work problem this week, you're practicing something much bigger. To help with that "mental space" concern, it might be worth choosing one specific moment — like a trip to the bathroom or a minute before a stressful meeting — to anchor the practice, so your brain doesn't have to remember it from scratch in the middle of the storm.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
